Reticulate knifefish (Papyrocranus afer) attains a maximum recorded total length of 80 cm [Li = 80 cm], a size that places it among the larger members of the Notopteridae family. This ultimate total length is based on field measurements of adult specimens from West African river systems, where the species is most abundant. The wet weight at birth of newly hatched individuals is remarkably small, with freshly emerged prolarvae weighing just 0.0244 grams [Wwb = 0.0244 grams], a value derived from the estimated egg diameter of 3.6 millimeters. This minuscule initial mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the lecithotrophic yolk-sac larva, which must rapidly transition to exogenous feeding. The incubation period leading to eclosion is relatively brief. When maintained at a stable temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the yolk-sac larva emerges from the chorion after approximately 17 days [ab = approximately 17 days], a developmental duration that is consistent with incubation times observed in other tropical teleosts with small eggs.

Substantial changes in body composition occur as the individual progresses through the juvenile stage towards sexual maturation. The total length at puberty for this species has been estimated at roughly 40 cm [Lp = roughly 40 cm], although some published accounts have reported values closer to 53.4 cm for the 50 percent maturity threshold. However, local field data from the Lindi-Nkanda system indicate that 40 cm is a more reliable benchmark for the onset of gonadal recrudescence. Corresponding to this length, the estimated wet weight at puberty is 162.5 g [Wwp = 162.5 g]rams, a mass that represents the accumulation of considerable somatic tissue during the growing juvenile phase. This pubertal body mass is derived from an allometric relationship with the ultimate length and maximum body mass of the species. During this sub-adult period, individuals shift from a diet dominated by aquatic invertebrates to incorporating a greater proportion of small fish, fueling the rapid growth necessary to reach reproductive size.

The maximum body mass documented for adult Reticulate knifefish is 1.3 kilograms [Wwi = 1.3 kilograms], a substantial wet weight achieved only by the largest and oldest individuals in the population. This ultimate wet weight contrasts sharply with the neonatal mass of 0.0244 grams, representing a remarkable increase in body size over the lifespan. A gravid female approaching this maximum mass may produce several thousand eggs during a single spawning event, though fecundity scales with body size. The species is iteroparous, with mature individuals likely spawning multiple times across consecutive breeding seasons. Under the same thermal conditions used for incubation studies, at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the maximum lifespan of this knifefish has been recorded as 30 years [am = 30 years], an exceptionally long life for a freshwater teleost of its size, likely related to the relatively stable and low-predation environments of deep river channels.

Reproductive investment in the Reticulate knifefish reflects its life-history strategy as a large-bodied, long-lived species. Females produce adhesive eggs that are deposited on submerged vegetation or hard substrates, with the male typically guarding the nest until the larvae hatch. The total length at which puberty is attained, 40 cm [Lp = 40 cm], may be reached only after several years of growth, given the relatively slow developmental pace characteristic of the species. A female of that length will typically have a wet weight at puberty of 162.5 g [Wwp = 162.5 g]rams, a figure that serves as a useful predictor of first reproductive output. The species is believed to spawn once annually during the flood season. Each breeding event yields a clutch of eggs. Field observations indicate that a female of average size deposits approximately 2,000 eggs per clutch. The same reproductively active female will produce a single clutch each year, constrained by the seasonal availability of flooded spawning grounds.

Longevity records for the Reticulate knifefish confirm a maximum lifespan of 30 years [am = 30 years] under natural conditions, a duration that is particularly noteworthy among African freshwater fish at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This extended lifespan, combined with the modest clutch size of approximately 2,000 eggs, suggests a life-history strategy oriented toward adult survival rather than high fecundity. In laboratory aquaria maintained at a water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the yolk-sac larva hatches after an incubation period of roughly 17 days [ab = roughly 17 days], identical to the development time documented in wild settings at comparable temperatures. The age at birth is therefore consistent across environments when thermal conditions are equivalent. Captive individuals have been known to survive for up to three decades, confirming the maximum lifespan estimate derived from field mark-recapture studies. This exceptional longevity may be an adaptation to the unpredictable hydrological regimes of West African rivers, where years of low rainfall can suppress recruitment, placing a premium on the survival of established adults.
